transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Sharma (Redwood SE), Sara Kim (Helix PL), Diego Alvarez (Helix ML Infra), Nadia Patel (Helix Security)

Summary: short technical deep dive focused on throughput tuning for Helix's private deployment: continuous batching behavior, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, slot sizes), token limits, KV cache warmup, and quantization trade-offs. Discussed on-prem VPC constraints and benchmarking plan.

Topics: continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, KV cache, quantization (4-bit/8-bit), on-prem/VPC I/O, measurement and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this pretty focused — intent is to go through throughput knobs and then map that to your profile.
[00:14] Sara: thanks, Alex. quick intro, i'm sara, platform lead at Helix. main goal is to get 99th perc latency under 500ms for our chat endpoints with cost predictability.
[00:26] Priya: hey, Priya from Redwood se, i'll drive the runtime bits. diego, can you confirm the baseline you're seeing today?
[00:32] Diego: yeah so baseline is kinda a mixed bag — on our prod-ish cluster we get about 120 qps peak across 8 gpus, avg seq len 64, p95 token latency about 1.2s, and we saw KV cache hit rate very low ~5% because prompts vary a lot.
[00:52] Nadia: also to note security constraint — must run in our VPC, no external kv caching allowed, and keys stored in our KMS.
[01:05] Alex: got it. a few high-level levers: batching (continuous batching in Redwood), scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs and max_tokens per batch, token caps per request, kv cache priming and pinning, and quantization level. we'll walk through tuning each.
[01:26] Priya: starting with continuous batching — our runtime keeps a short window (milliseconds) to coalesce requests and form batching groups based on seq count and token budget. default is aggressive for hosted, but on-prem you might want to tune the window and max_num_seqs to balance latency vs throughput.
[01:45] Diego: can you explain max_num_seqs? we saw a config but not sure mapping to GPU occupancy.
[01:51] Priya: max_num_seqs is the maximum number of concurrent sequences in a single scheduler batch. in effect it caps batch size; higher value increases GPU utilization but increases tail latency because some requests wait to fill batch. with short seqs (avg 64) a higher max_num_seqs (e.g., 64-128) can give much better throughput. with long seqs you might be CPU/memory bound earlier.
[02:18] Sara: our workload has a bimodal distribution — some sessions are short (10-30 tokens) and some are long (200-400 tokens) for transcript generation. how to handle that?
[02:28] Priya: two approaches: 1) schedule by sequence-length buckets (fast path for short seqs) or 2) set separate queue priorities, we can create a low-latency queue that has small max_num_seqs and tight token caps, and a throughput queue that is more permissive. Redwood supports per-route scheduler policies.
[02:46] Alex: we often recommend using a small low-latency route for interactive chat and a separate background route for long-running transcript generation. that keeps your 99th down.
[02:59] Diego: what about continuous batching window? we saw 'batch_wait_ms' in config, what's a good starting point?
[03:05] Priya: start with 5-10ms for interactive routes, 20-50ms for throughput routes. small windows are lower latency but lower batch sizes. also the runtime has adaptive batching that widens window at low load to collect more sequences.
[03:21] Sara: ok. KV cache — our main hope is reuse across sessions, but prompts vary because of personalization. any pragmatic tips?
[03:29] Priya: KV cache reuse is highest when you have repeated prefixes — e.g., system prompts, assistant priming, or repeated doc retrieval context. to improve hit rate you can: 1) canonicalize prompts (strip ephemeral tokens), 2) shard cache by customer/session or by prompt fingerprint, 3) use a warmup phase where common recent prompts are pre-primed. note for VPC/on-prem, cache resides in instance memory not external if you need isolation.
[03:56] Diego: we can't use external cache per security, so in-memory KV across requests is the plan — any memory sizing guidelines?
[04:04] Priya: KV cache grows with num_beams * seq_len * hidden_dim; a rough heuristic: for a 3B-ish model, each token vector ~3-4KB unquantized, with quantization it's smaller. we can share cache across replicas if you use a shared state approach but that adds network overhead. usually you provision extra GPU memory headroom (20-30%) to hold hot KV.
[04:28] Nadia: will that break our compliance since keys in memory? we need KMS + encrypted memory.
[04:34] Alex: Redwood's private offers KMS integration and optional encrypted RAM at the host level; we'll send the security doc showing KMS and audit logs.
[04:42] Sara: quantization — do you recommend 4-bit for our workload? tradeoffs?
[04:48] Priya: 4-bit quant (awq/llm.int8-like) gives big perf and memory wins but may have small quality regressions on some instruction tasks. recommended path: 8-bit as conservative, 4-bit for throughput routes where slight drop is acceptable. we also have hybrid where embeddings/encoder parts are left higher precision. we'll recommend a quick eval on your top-50 prompts.
[05:12] Diego: how about kernel selection and triton? we're using NVIDIA Triton for some endpoints now.
[05:18] Priya: Redwood runtime has its own kernel selection layer; for on-prem GPUs we pick optimized kernels (cuda/fused attention) and can integrate with Triton for model lifecycle, but mixing runtimes can add overhead. if you're already on Triton and happy, we can benchmark both; often our runtime wins on multi-request batching because of optimized KV and scheduler.
[05:40] Alex: let's talk about token limits per batch — there is max_tokens_per_batch (or token_budget) which prevents very long sequences from starving short ones. set that lower on latency route.
[05:51] Priya: yes, token_budget prevents long sequences from causing OOM and reduces head-of-line blocking. you can also set per-request token cap so one long request doesn't fill batch budget.
[06:02] Diego: we saw occasional OOM at p99 — what's the recommended safety margin?
[06:08] Priya: we generally recommend reserving 10-15% of GPU memory for runtime and other processes, and configure soft OOM handlers to reject very long requests with 413-like error or re-route them to a background queue.
[06:21] Sara: metrics — what's the minimal telemetry we need to tune these knobs?
[06:25] Priya: capture: per-route qps, seq_len histogram, batch_size distribution, batch_wait_ms distribution, kv_cache_hit_rate, gpu_utilization, p50/p95/p99 token latency, and OOM/reject counts. Redwood console surfaces these but you can also export to prometheus.
[06:43] Diego: can we get a quick example config for a two-route setup?
[06:48] Alex: sure. high-level: route low-latency: max_num_seqs=16, token_budget=1024, batch_wait_ms=6. route throughput: max_num_seqs=128, token_budget=8192, batch_wait_ms=30, enable adaptive widening. i'll put the exact yaml in the playbook.
[07:08] Sara: what about autoscaling and burst capacity? we have diurnal spikes and short marketing driven bursts.
[07:15] Priya: autoscaling should be tied to queue latency or batch fill rate rather than raw qps; scale up when batch fill rate drops below threshold or 95th latency increases. for burst protection, Redwood supports burst pools that spin up additional capacity for a short window. On-prem? it depends on your infra — we can pre-allocate burst nodes in your VPC or use spot-like instances if acceptable.
[07:39] Diego: for on-prem we want deterministic performance, so pre-allocated is preferred. how fast does the runtime recover after scale-up?
[07:45] Priya: cold-start time depends on model size and quantization; with cached model artifacts and warm kernels you can be ready in 30-90s for medium models; with larger ones it can take longer. pre-warmed nodes with model loaded gives near-instant capacity.
[07:59] Nadia: security question — if we enable shared KV across replicas, does that leak cross-tenant data?
[08:05] Alex: by default KV is tenant-scoped. cross-replica shared KV is only for intra-customer replication and is encrypted; we never mix tenant data. we'll include a section in the security doc.
[08:16] Diego: curious about measurement experiments — what's a good bench plan to show improvement after tuning?
[08:21] Priya: two-stage plan: stage 1 baseline capture (1-2 hrs at representative load) with full telemetry. stage 2 knob sweep offline on a staging cluster (vary max_num_seqs, batch_wait_ms, token_budget, quantization) and capture p50/p95/p99, throughput, GPU utilization. stage 3 validate at low percent of prod traffic (canary) and then ramp. we'll provide scripts for running these sweeps.
[08:48] Sara: can you share the scripts?
[08:50] Alex: yes, included in the playbook we'll send.
[08:54] Diego: one last nuance — what about request coalescing when requests have different model variants? we have both a 7B optimized and a 13B fallback.
[09:03] Priya: runtime groups compatible variants; we can configure compatibility sets so that 7B and quant 13B won't be coalesced. we also support fallback routing where an overloaded tier routes to a cheaper model but with controlled degradation.
[09:20] Sara: perfect. recap of concrete next steps?
[09:24] Alex: recap: 1) Alex send tuning playbook + example configs + security doc by 2026-03-20. 2) Diego provide representative traffic histogram and sample prompts by 2026-03-22. 3) Priya prepare KV cache priming runbook and perf sweep scripts by 2026-03-25. 4) schedule on-prem pilot week of 2026-03-30.
[09:45] Nadia: sounds good. small ask: include notes on compliance and memory encryption.
[09:50] Alex: will do.
[09:54] Sara: thanks all, this was helpful.
[09:58] Alex: thanks, we'll follow up.
